title: PARLIAMENT QUESTION: ZERO LITIGATION PENSION ECOSYSTEM
body_text:
The Department of Pension and Pensioners' Welfare is the nodal Department for formulation of policies relating to pension and other retirement benefits of Central Government Civil employees. The 2nd National Workshop on Pension Litigation was convened in pursuance of Government's directives on effective and efficient management of litigation with focus on enhancing coordination and strengthening the capacity/skills of the Nodal officers and panel lawyers of all the Ministries/Departments handling Pension related litigation and its monitoring. It had deliberations and presentations from speakers on the best practices, systemic reforms and grievance redressals to minimize pension litigation towards welfare of pensioners and good governance. The Compendium of case laws and flyer, launched in the Workshop, outlined the best practices in handling pension litigation and recent judicial pronouncements in recurring pension litigation matters providing a comprehensive overview of the concerned pension related policies.
The compendium and flyer underscored the importance of a coordinated approach to managing pension litigation. Pension litigation is not centrally handled by any Department, it is handled on behalf of the Central Government separately by all respective Departments. For minimising litigation, Special Campaign 3 was also launched, wherein focus is on the redressal of the long pending grievances/claims and the issues. This campaign along with other initiatives viz. Pension Adalats and Inter-Ministerial Review Meetings on long pending grievances is an attempt to resolve the grievances, thereby obviating the need to approach courts of law with the resultant effect of reduction in litigation. Further, the Department, based on the clarification and advices sought by various Ministries and Departments, issues Office Memoranda to clarify the rule position to bring ease in the life of the pensioners including super-senior pensioners. The Department, has issued the Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 1972 revised it further by CCS(Pension) Rules, 2021. To ease eligibility conditions of family pensioners, Rule 50 of the said Rules (erstwhile Rule 54 of Rules of 1972) has been provided for various categories of family pensioners including divorced and disabled daughters.
This information was given by the Minister of State (Ind. Charge) Science & Technology; Earth Sciences and Minister of State PMO; Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions; Department of Atomic Energy and Space Dr. Jitendra Singh in a written reply in Rajya Sabha today.

ministry.name: Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances & Pensions

enrichment.summary: In a written Rajya Sabha reply, Union Minister Dr. Jitendra Singh described government efforts to build a 'zero litigation' pension ecosystem, highlighting the 2nd National Workshop on Pension Litigation organised by the Department of Pension and Pensioners' Welfare (DoPPW). The workshop launched a Compendium of case laws and an explanatory flyer on best practices in pension litigation, alongside 'Special Campaign 3' aimed at resolving long-pending pension grievances. The reply also referenced Pension Adalats, Inter-Ministerial Review Meetings, and the CCS (Pension) Rules 2021, which replaced the 1972 Rules and eased eligibility conditions for family pensioners including divorced and disabled daughters under Rule 50.
enrichment.context:
Pension litigation in India has historically been fragmented, with each Ministry/Department separately defending cases before courts and tribunals rather than a centralized body handling all pension disputes, leading to inconsistent interpretations and repeated litigation on similar issues. The Department of Pension and Pensioners' Welfare (DoPPW), under the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, is the nodal agency for policy on retirement benefits for Central Government civil employees and has been pushing systemic reforms—such as Pension Adalats (grievance redressal camps), inter-ministerial review meetings, and now litigation management workshops—to reduce the burden on courts and improve pensioner welfare, in line with the broader 'Minimum Government, Maximum Governance' and ease-of-living agenda.

The CCS (Pension) Rules 2021 replaced the older 1972 Rules, incorporating administrative reforms and clarifications addressing modern family structures and social realities, such as extending family pension eligibility to divorced and disabled daughters, which reflects a progressive expansion of welfare coverage. Special Campaigns for grievance redressal (like Special Campaign 3, part of a series across ministries) and centralized documentation such as compendiums of case law are tools to standardize practice, prevent frivolous or repetitive litigation, and align administrative decisions with judicial precedent—key aspects of good governance and administrative reform relevant to GS Paper 2.

prelims_questions.question: The Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 2021 replaced which earlier set of rules governing pensions of Central Government civil employees?
prelims_questions.explanation: The release states that the Department issued the CCS (Pension) Rules, 1972, which was further revised by the CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021.

prelims_questions.question: Which of the following categories of family pensioners is specifically mentioned as covered under Rule 50 of the CCS (Pension) Rules, 2021 (erstwhile Rule 54 of the 1972 Rules)?
prelims_questions.explanation: The release explicitly mentions that Rule 50 provides eligibility for various categories of family pensioners including divorced and disabled daughters.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the significance of a coordinated litigation management strategy in reducing pension-related disputes in India. In this context, evaluate the role of initiatives such as Pension Adalats, Special Campaigns, and compendiums of case law.
Examine how recent reforms in pension rules, such as the CCS (Pension) Rules 2021, reflect an evolving understanding of family structures and social welfare needs in India.
